signs.text: THE LOOM. A Hattersley double-width loom, a hundred years old and still going. Treadles below, shuttle across, beam forward, and again, thousands of times for one length of cloth. Harris Tweed is woven on looms like this in the islanders' own homes, often in a shed beside the house.

signs.title: Òrain Luaidh
signs.text: Waulking songs, òrain luaidh, were sung by women finishing the tweed: the wet cloth was thumped and passed round a long board to shrink and soften it, and the singing kept the rhythm, one woman leading a verse and the rest answering with the chorus. The songs ran to love, gossip, boats and the men who had not come home, and a good waulking could last all evening. The mill does the shrinking now. The songs are still sung, often by people with cleaner hands.
